items.title: Herdr (AI Agent Multiplexer)r: You're not a PRO AI Coder if you're not using THIS OPENSOURCE Tool!
items.summary:
Visit Verdent: https://www.verdent.ai/?id=700712

Visit AISeeKing (my second channel with more cool local ai stuff): https://www.youtube.com/@AISeeKing

In this video, I'll be telling you about Herdr, a terminal-based agent multiplexer built for running multiple AI coding agents at the same time. It works like tmux for the AI agent era, with live agent state tracking, persistent sessions, remote mode, and an automation API that lets agents coordinate with each other.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Herdr is an agent-native terminal multiplexer designed for managing multiple AI coding agents.
🧠 It can detect whether agents are working, blocked, idle, or done across different panes.
🖥️ You still get familiar multiplexer features like spaces, tabs, split panes, and persistent sessions.
🤖 Herdr supports many agent CLIs, including Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, Cursor Agent, and more.
🔔 Background notifications help you know when an agent is blocked or finished without babysitting panes.
🛠
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi. Welcome to another video. Before starting the video, I'd like to tell you that I have become more active on my AI Seeking channel now. I am posting some new stuff and some developer-related tools that I don't cover here. So, you can go ahead and check it out as well. I'll put the link to it in the description. So, if you run AI coding agents seriously, your setup probably looks something like this. One Claude code session doing a refactor, one Codec session fixing a bug, maybe an open code or Gemini CLI session doing research, and all of it spread across a bunch of terminal tabs or tmux panes. And the real problem is not running the agents. The real problem is knowing what they are doing. Is that agent still working? Is it sitting there blocked on a permission prompt for the last 10 minutes while you were looking at another pane? Did it finish 20 minutes ago? Tmux has no idea because to tmux, an AI agent is just another process. And that is exactly the problem Herder is built to solve. So, Herder is basically an agent multiplexer that lives in your terminal. It is written in Rust. It runs inside your existing terminal instead of replacing it. And the whole point of it is that it actually understands AI coding agents. It knows when an agent is working, when it is blocked and waiting on you, when it is idle, and when it is done. And on top of that, it gives your agents a CLI and a socket API so they can orchestrate each other, which is where things get really interesting for pro users. If you ask me, this is one of the most agent-native takes on terminal multiplexing that I have seen yet. So, let's get right into it. Now, the first thing to understand is what Herder actually is. Think of it like tmux, but rebuilt from scratch for the agent era. You get workspaces, which Herder calls spaces, you get tabs, you get split panes, and you get persistent sessions that survive disconnects. So, all the normal multiplexer stuff is there. But then there is a sidebar that lists every agent it has detected across all your panes along with its live state. So, instead of cycling through panes like a helicopter parent to check on each agent, you just glance at the sidebar and immediately see which one needs you. That alone changes how many agents you can realistically run in parallel. And the agent support is genuinely broad. Herder detects around 20 agent CLIs out of the box. Claude code, Codex open code, cursor agent, Copilot CLI, grok CLI, Quen code, kilo code, droid amp, Devin Kiro, and a bunch more. Gemini CLI and Cline are also detected, although those are a bit less tested. And even if your agent is not on the list, it still runs fine as a normal terminal process. You just do not get the rich state tracking for it. So, it is not locking you into any one vendor's stack, which I always like to see. Installation is simple, too. On a Mac, you can just run brew install herder. On Linux, there is a one-line curl install script from their website. There is a PowerShell script for Windows. And if you are a Rust person, you can also do cargo install herder. Once it is installed, you just type herder in your terminal and you are in. And because it renders inside your existing terminal, your fonts, your colors, and your shell config all stay exactly as they are. The interface itself is honestly quite friendly. If you have used tmux, you already know the basics because the prefix key is control B by default. Control B and a question mark shows you all the key bindings, and you can split panes, create tabs, and make new spaces from there. But, unlike tmux, the mouse is a first-class citizen. You can click panes to focus them, drag to resize, and right-click for context menus to split or close panes. So, you get tmux-style muscle memory if you want it without the usual prefix key gymnastics if you do not. Now, let's talk about the state tracking because this is the core feature, and it is worth understanding how it actually works. Herder tracks four states for each agent. Working means the agent is actively processing. Blocked means it is waiting on you. So, a permission prompt, a question, an approval. Idle means it is sitting there ready for a prompt. And done means it finished a task and you have not looked at it yet. That last one is a nice detail because the difference between idle and done is basically whether you have actually seen the result. So, a finished agent stays flagged until you review it instead of quietly blending back into the noise. And under the hood, there are two detection mechanisms. For some agents, Hurder uses proper life cycle hooks where the agent itself reports its state directly. That is the most accurate signal. For agents that do not have full hooks like Claude Code, it watches the bottom of the terminal buffer and matches it against known UI patterns using detection rules. So, when Claude Code throws up a permission prompt, Hurder recognizes that visually and marks the agent as blocked. And they have deliberately made blocked detection conservative, so it only fires when it actually matches a known approval or question UI instead of spamming you with false alarm. To get the best tracking, you can install per agent integrations. You just run Hurder integration install Claude and it wires up the Claude Code integration for you. There is also a Hurder integration status command to see what is active. And once integrations are in place, you can also get notifications when an agent in a background pane changes state. So, you can be heads down in one pane and when your background agent finishes or gets blocked, Hurder pings you. No more babysitting. This is pretty amazing for parallel work, to be honest. Now, let's come to the part that I think pro agent users will care about the most, which is the automation layer. Hurder exposes a CLI and a local socket API. And here is the key thing. Your agents can call it, too. So, an agent running inside Hurder can split panes, start other agents, prompt them, wait for them to finish, and read their output, which means Hurder is not just a viewer for your agents. It is an orchestration surface. Let me walk you through what that looks like. There are pane commands. So, pane split with a direction, pane run to execute a command, pane send text and send keys for raw input, pane wait output to wait for a pattern, and pane read to grab the output back. Then there are agent commands. Agent start launches a supported agent in a pane with the {double-dash} kind flag, so Codex, Claude, Gemini, Cursor, and so on. Agent prompt submits a prompt, and you can add the {double-dash} wait flag to block until it reaches a target state. Agent wait waits for a state like idle, done, or blocked. Agent read pulls the agent's recent output, and agent rename gives an agent a stable name like reviewer or tester, so you can address it by name instead of by pane ID. So, here's a concrete workflow. You are in Claude Code, and you tell it something like, "Implement this feature." And when you're done, spin up a Codex agent in a new pane and have it review your diff. Claude Code can then literally run Herder pane split to create a pane on the right, run Herder agent start reviewer with the {double-dash} kind Codex flag, then Herder agent prompt reviewer with the review instructions and the {double-dash} wait flag. And once the reviewer is done, it runs Herder agent read reviewer to pull the feedback back in and address it. One prompt from you, and two agents coordinated the whole thing between themselves. This is the kind of multi-agent pipeline that people usually duct tape together with tmux send keys and a prayer. Here it is just a supported first-class API. Chef's kiss. Really good stuff. Now, let me quickly show you how this fits into my actual workflow, because I do not run everything in the terminal. The way I split things these days is pretty simple. The bigger, well-defined project work goes to Verdant, and the faster, terminal-native tasks live in my Herder setup. So, on one side, I have Verdant deck open. I give it a bigger goal like building out a whole feature, and it plans the project properly, breaks it down into tasks, and then runs its own parallel agents on it, each in an isolated session. It keeps the whole project in context, and I just review the diffs when the tasks are ready. I do not have to wire any of that up myself because that planning and delegation layer is just built in. And if I'm away from my desk, I can even send it instructions from Slack or Telegram, and it keeps working. You can also use it through their VS Code or JetBrains extensions if you prefer that. And it lets you pick between different top models, including some free ones. And on the other side, Herder is running my terminal herd. Claude Code doing a refactor, Codex on review duty, a pane with tests and logs. The Herder sidebar tells me when a terminal agent is blocked or done, and Verdant tells me when its tasks are ready for review. So, between those two, I am basically never babysitting anything. Verdant handles the planned delegated work, and Herder keeps the ad hoc terminal work visible. And honestly, this combination is what parallel agent work is supposed to feel like. If you want to try that setup, Verdant has a free trial right now, and it is linked below. Anyway, now let's come to the other big pillar of Herder, which is persistence. And this one matters a lot if you run long agent sessions. Herder uses a client-server model. So, the server holds the real terminals, and your client just attaches to it. You can detach with control BQ, close your laptop, come back later, run Herder again, and everything is still running. Your agents never stopped. And if the server itself restarts, Herder restores your session shape, so your spaces, tabs, panes, working directories, and layout all come back. But here is the part I really like. Herder also does native agent session restore. So, for supported agents, after a restart, it can resume the actual agent conversation automatically using things like the resume functionality in Claude Code under the hood, which means a server restart does not mean losing your agent's context. That is enabled by default, and you can turn it off in the config if you want. There is also an experimental pane history replay feature that saves terminal output across restarts, although it is off by default because your scrollback can contain secrets and tokens, which is a fair call. And then there's remote mode, which extends all of this to other machines. You can run Hurder with the {dash} {dash} remote flag pointing at an SSH host, and the server runs on the remote box, while the client stays local. So, your agents run on your beefy dev server or your VPs with its files and its compute, but your local keybindings and theme still apply, and you can detach and reattach from anywhere. Combine that with the persistent story, and you can basically leave a herd of agents running on a server overnight and check on them from any machine. There is even an experimental live handoff feature that can keep processes alive across server updates. So, they are clearly taking the always running angle seriously. Configuration is pretty straightforward as well. Everything lives in a config file in your {dot} config Hurder folder. You can change the prefix key to something like control space if you want, tweak the sidebar, configure notifications and scrollback, and pick from built-in themes like Catppuccin, Gruvbox, Nord, and Dracula. And you can reload the config in a running session without restarting anything. There is also a plugin system with a marketplace where plugins are basically local executables with manifest actions and event hooks. It is still early, but the direction is nice. Now, I do have to mention the limitations because there are some. First, this is pre-1.0 software. It is moving fast, and protocol upgrades between versions can require stopping the running server, which kills your panes. That is exactly the kind of rough edge you accept with young tools. Second, for agents without lifecycle hooks, including Claude code right now, state detection is based on screen matching. It is conservative and works well in practice, but it is still heuristics, not a direct signal. Third, Windows support is behind Mac and Linux, and a Windows machine cannot be a remote target yet. And fourth, if you run tmux inside a Hurder pane, agent detection inside that tmux session breaks, which makes sense, but it means you should let Hurder be the multiplexer instead of nesting things. So, it is not perfect, but none of these are deal breakers for what it is trying to do. Overall, I think Herder nails a very real problem. The bottleneck with parallel agents was never starting them. It was tracking them and coordinating them. And Herder gives you state awareness in a sidebar, notifications when something needs you, an API that lets agents orchestrate each other, sessions that survive disconnects and restarts with the agent context intact, and remote mode on top. Plus, it is free and open source, works with basically every terminal agent out there, and takes a couple of minutes to set up. If you only ever run one agent at a time, tmux or even a plain terminal is honestly fine. And you do not need this. But if you are the kind of person who has three or four agents going in parallel, this is the closest thing to a proper mission control for them that I have seen in the terminal. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.

items.title: Qwen 3.8 Flash Next (Fully Tested & VS GLM-5.3 Flash): You can run it LOCALLY! & IT"S CRAZY!
items.summary:
Visit AISeeKing (my second channel with more cool local ai stuff): https://www.youtube.com/@AISeeKing

In this video, I'll be testing Alibaba’s new Qwen 3.8 Flash Next model, which is an experimental preview of the upcoming Qwen 4 architecture. It’s a 125-billion-parameter MoE model that only activates 6 billion parameters per token, making it extremely cheap and efficient, while still offering strong agentic, math, and long-context performance.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Alibaba released Qwen 3.8 Flash Next as an experimental preview of the future Qwen 4 architecture.
⚡ It is a 125B parameter MoE model, but only activates 6B parameters per token for very low compute cost.
💸 The API pricing is extremely cheap at 16 cents per million input tokens and 47 cents per million output tokens.
🧠 The model uses a hybrid architecture with Gated DeltaNet blocks and Qwen Sparse Attention for long-context efficiency.
📚 Around 51B parameters are used for bigram and trigram embeddings, which can sit in reg
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: Hi, welcome to another video. Before starting the video, I'd like to tell you that I have become more active on my AIC King channel. Now, I am posting some new stuff and some developer related tools that I don't cover here. So, you can go ahead and check it out as well. I'll put the link to it in the description. So, a couple of days ago, Alibaba released a new model called QN 3.8 Flash Next. This is not just another QN model. It's basically an experimental preview of the new architecture that they are going to use in Q4. So you can think of it as a sneak peek into what the next generation of QN models is going to look like. The model is a 125 billion parameter MOI model. But here's the crazy part. It only activates 6 billion parameters per token. Just 6 billion. That's why they are calling it flash next. It's built for ultimate cost efficiency and the pricing shows that as well. The API costs just 16 cents per million input tokens and 47 cents per million output tokens, which is about 12 times cheaper than QN 3.8 max. Alibaba is also claiming that it delivers better results than QN 3.7 plus at roughly 1 nth of the training cost, which is just insane if true. It's fully open weights as well and it's available on hugging phase under the QN community license. So, this is quite great to see. Now let's talk about the architecture because this is where things get really interesting. The first big change is the attention system. Instead of using full attention everywhere, they are using a hybrid setup. The model has 48 layers and they follow a repeating pattern. Three gated delta blocks which are linear attention and then one block of something new called QN sparse attention or QSA. Each of these is paired with ane layer. The interesting thing about QSA is that instead of selecting individual tokens like other sparse attention methods, it operates at the microblock level. This reduces latency a lot, especially for long context and agentic workloads where the model is churning through massive amounts of tokens. The second big change is the engram embedding layer. This one is really unique. Out of the 125 billion parameters, around 51 billion are just bgram and trigram embeddings. You can think of it as a phrase dictionary baked into the model. Common word groups get stored as distinct entries so the model doesn't have to compute them from scratch every time. And the best part is that this layer can sit in normal RAM instead of GPU memory. It's basically a way to scale up the parameter count without scaling up the compute. And it's much better suited for memory constrained hardware. On top of that, you get the MOI setup with 512 experts, out of which 11 are activated per token. There's also multi-token prediction for faster inference and gated residuals for training stability. The context length is 262k tokens natively, and it can be extended to 1 million tokens with Yarn. It's also a thinking model by default, so it generates reasoning before answering, but you can turn that off if you want. On the official benchmarks, Alibaba is claiming some big numbers. They say it beats Clawed Opus 4.6 6 on Swaybench Pro with 62.5 versus 53.4 and it scores 91.7 on GPQA Diamond. They are also claiming that it beats Deepseek V4 Flash on coding tasks, which is a much bigger model with 284 billion parameters and 13 billion activated. But these are vendor benchmarks, so take them with a grain of salt. That's exactly why I run my own tests. So, let's get right into the benchmarks and see how it actually performs on Kingbench. As always, I tested it on my eight questions, and each question is scored out of 10. So, the maximum score is 80. I'll also be comparing it against GLM 5.3 Flash throughout because that's its direct competitor in the fast and cheap category. The first question is the elevator simulation. The model has to create three elevators, spawn people on different levels, and each elevator can only take one person. The people should also have tool types with their floor numbers, and it should all be well animated. Quen 3.8 flash next scored a five on this one. The basic logic was there, but the animations were janky and the one person per elevator rule wasn't handled properly in all cases. GLM 5.3 flash got a six here, so slightly better. The second question is the 3JS contact lens case. It needs pronounced L and R caps that you can click to open. Flash Next actually did quite well here and scored an eight. The caps were clickable, the model looked decent, and the geometry was mostly right. GLM 5.3 Flash got a seven on this one. So, Flash Next actually wins this test. So, that's great. The third question is the 3JS folding table with a slider that folds and unfolds it. And this is where things fell apart. Flash Next only scored a two here. The table barely resembled a table and the folding motion was completely broken. GLM 5.3 Flash scored a seven on the same test. So, this is a big gap. This is a fail for sure. The fourth question is the SVG of a panda eating a burger. Flash next got a six. The panda was recognizable. The burger was kind of there, but it wasn't winning any art contests. GLM 5.3. Flash got an eight here. So again, a bit better on the visual side. The fifth question is the bow and arrow simulator game with four targets and a leaderboard. Flash next scored an eight and GLM 5.3. Flash also scored an eight. Both did a good job here. The game worked. The targets were hitable and the leaderboard logic was fine. So this one is a tie. The sixth question is the hard math problem about counting permutations of ordered pairs. And the answer should be 2460. Flash next. A full 10. GLM 5.3 flash also got a 10. To be honest, most of the newer models are getting this one right now, but it's still good to see a 6B active parameter model doing competition level math. The seventh question is the agentic one. The model has to generate a data set of pandemma 2B model on it and then create a local web UI that generates a pandifact on every refresh all on its own. Flash. Next got a full 10 on this. It did the whole pipeline without any handholding, which is pretty amazing for a model this cheap. GLM 5.3 Flash also got a 10 here. The Aenta capabilities on both of these are really solid. The eighth question is the 3D wristwatch that works based on the current time with smooth hands, a date and day option, and dual time zone tracking. Flash Next got a seven and GLM 5.3 Flash also got a seven. Both made working watches, but neither was perfect on the full wristwatch. Look, this is the final chart and Quen 3.8 flash next ends up with 56 out of 80, which is 70%. GLM 5.3 Flash sits at 63 out of 80, which is 78.75%. So, what does this tell us on my leaderboard? Flash Next lands in the middle of the pack. It's above GPT 5.6, Luna, Sonnet 5, and Gro 4.5, which is honestly impressive for 6 billion active parameters. But GLM 5.3 Flash is still clearly ahead of it, mainly because of the visual and 3D stuff. If you look at where the points were lost, it's almost all front-end polish. The folding table alone costed five points against GLM. On math and aentic tasks, they are dead even with both getting perfect scores. For context, the big GLM 5.3 is still at the top of my leaderboard with 91.25% and even QN's own 3.8 Max is at 81.25%. So flash next is not going to replace your main coding model but as a cheap fast model for agentic pipelines tool calling and long context work. It's a really good option for sure. Now let's talk about running it locally because this is where the architecture actually pays off. The weights are on hugging face and there's an official FP8 version as well. Unsloth has already released GGUF quants and here's what the sizes look like. The one bit dynamic quants are around 72 to 74 gigs. The 2-bit is about 79 gigs. The 3-bit versions are 82 to 90 gigs. And the 4-bit ones go from about 94 gigs up to 111 gigs. So, yes, it's a big download. Either way, you're realistically looking at 96 to 128 gigs of RAM to run this thing comfortably. A 128 gig Mac with unified memory would be the sweet spot, or a PC with 128 gigs of RAM and a decent GPU where you offload the experts to system memory. But here's the thing. Because only 6 billion parameters are active per token, the actual compute per token is tiny. And remember that 51 billion parameter n layer I mentioned. It's designed to sit in regular RAM. So unlike a dense 70b model that crawls on CPU, this one can actually generate at usable speeds even without stacking multiple GPUs. It's memory hungry but compute light. That's the whole trade-off of this architecture. To run it, the easiest way is Olama. You can just run olamarun followed by hf.co/unsloth/qn3.8 flash nextguf with a colon and the quant name at the end. If you want an openi compatible server, you can use llama.cp and run the llama serve command with the - hf flag pointing to the same repo. And if you have real hardware, vlm and sglang are the recommended options for production. And if you don't have that kind of RAM, honestly, the API at 16 cents per million input tokens is so cheap that it's hard to justify the hardware. Anyway, overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. Heat. Heat.

In this video, I'll be telling you about the Ox Alpha reveal, which Z AI has now officially confirmed as GLM 5.3 Flash. The model is open-weight under an MIT license, extremely cheap through the API, and may be one of the best options yet for running a frontier-adjacent AI model locally.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Z AI has officially revealed that the Ox Alpha stealth model was GLM 5.3 Flash.
🔓 GLM 5.3 Flash has been released on Hugging Face with full weights under an MIT license.
🧠 The model is a 320B parameter mixture-of-experts model with only 18B active parameters per token.
💸 API pricing is extremely cheap at 15 cents per million input tokens and 50 cents per million output tokens.
📊 On KingBench, GLM 5.3 Flash scored 63 out of 80, slightly below its stealth Ox Alpha score.

items.title: Unlazy: The SIMPLE Skill that actually improves PERFORMANCE of ALL AI AGENTS!!
items.summary:
Visit AISeeKing: https://www.youtube.com/@AISeeKing

In this video, I'll be telling you about unlazy, a GitHub repo designed to fix one of the biggest problems in AI coding right now: agents confidently saying work is done when the code is incomplete, untested, or full of placeholders. It introduces runnable acceptance gates, evidence-based verification, approval safety, and orchestration workflows to make AI agent completion much more reliable.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 unlazy helps AI coding agents prove completion with runnable acceptance gates instead of vague “done” reports.
📋 The GATES.md acceptance ledger defines observable outcomes, CHECK commands, EXPECT markers, and evidence lines.
✅ A gate only counts as met when the command exits successfully and the expected output is actually found.
🔒 The approval system prevents unreviewed shell commands from running and binds approvals to exact commands, paths, shells, and environments.
🔁 The --reverify mode re-runs gates instead of trustin
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi. Welcome to another video. Before starting the video, I'd like to tell you that I have become more active on my AIC King channel now. I am posting some new stuff and some developer-related tools that I don't cover here. So, you can go ahead and check it out as well. I'll put the link to it in the description. So, today I want to talk about a GitHub repo that attacks what is probably the single most annoying problem in AI coding right now. You give your agent a big task, it works for a while, and then it comes back with a super confident done. Everything is implemented and tested, and then you actually look at the code and half of it is placeholders. The tests were never run, and two of the five things you asked for are just missing. The repo is called Unlazy by Leon X LNX, and it is basically completion discipline for AI agents backed by runnable checks. The tagline is, "Write the acceptance ledger first, execute reviewed checks, re-verify returned work, and report only what the evidence supports." And I think this is one of the more thoughtful takes on this problem that I have seen yet. So, let's get right into it. At its core, Unlazy is a skill. It works with Claude code and Codex CLI, and the whole thing is built on plain node with zero third-party runtime packages. You just need Node 16 or newer. The current source targets version 2.1.0, and it is MIT licensed. The main idea is that instead of trusting the agent's own done report, you make completion testable. Before the agent does any real work, it has to write a file called gates.md. This is the acceptance ledger. Each gate in it is one observable outcome, and every runnable gate gets two things: a check line, which is an actual shell command, and an expect line, which is a success marker that has to show up in the output. A gate only counts as met when two conditions are true. The check command exits with code zero, and the expect text actually matches the combined output. When that happens, the checker writes an evidence line into the ledger with the resolved shell, the working directory, the exit status, a path fingerprint, and the decisive output. So, the agent cannot just tick a checkbox and call it a day. A checkbox with missing or pending evidence counts as unmet. And if a gate turns out to be genuinely impossible, the agent is not allowed to silently delete it. It has to add an abandon line with a non-empty reason, and that abandon abandonment surfaced in the final report. This is kind of great because it flips the whole dynamic. The model does not get to grade its own homework anymore, the ledger does. Now, let me show you how to install it. The easiest way is through the skills CLI from Vercel Labs. You just run NPX skills add leong x/unlazy. You can add the dash g flag for a user-level install or the dash dash all flag to install it for every detected agent on your machine. If you want to do it manually, you just clone the repo into your skills folder. For Claude Code, that is the dot Claude skills folder in your home directory. For CodeX, it is the dot CodeX skills folder. Once it is in there, you can invoke it with the slash unlazy command in Claude Code or dollar unlazy in CodeX. It also has natural language triggers. So, phrases like tree five gates or literally do not stop until it is done will activate it as well. Now, let's talk about how a solo run actually works because the workflow here is pretty careful. And honestly, the security thinking is one of my favorite parts of this repo. You start by copying the leaf template into a gates.md file and filling in your gates. Then you run the gate check script with the dash dash status flag. This is a report only mode. It parses the ledger, tells you what is met and unmet, and it is guaranteed to never execute anything. And here is the important bit. Check lines are shell code. The readme is very explicit about this. So, before anything runs, you are supposed to actually read every command and every script those commands call. When you do a normal run on a fresh Oracle that has no approval record yet, the checker does not execute it. Instead, it prints the resolved command, the expectation, the working directory, the shell, and the path, and leaves it unexecuted. Once you have read everything and you're happy, you run it again with the {dash} {dash} approve flag, and that approves each exact pending command and then runs it. These approvals are stored outside your repository under a {dot} unlazy folder in your home directory. And each approval is bound to the exact ledger, the exact gate, the exact check and expect text, the resolved working directory and shell, the timeout, the platform, and the full inherited path. If any of those change even slightly, it needs approval again. So, if you pull an inherited ledger from some untrusted repo and a command got swapped out, it does not just silently run. That is really good design, to be honest. There is also a {dash} {dash} reverify flag, which reruns every runnable gate, including the ones already marked complete, because old evidence is not re-execution. This matters a lot for the orchestration side, which we will get to in a second. One more thing I want to highlight is the section on authoring gates that can fail honestly. The docs openly admit that the checker can only prove the command Oracle you declare. It cannot know whether your English gate title and your shell command actually mean the same thing. So, it pushes you toward gates that read the real artifact, print a success only marker after all assertions pass, and test negative checks against a known positive control. It even tells you not to copy a supplied number into expect as its own proof, but to measure it independently. That is the kind of nuance most make the AI less lazy prompts completely miss. Anyway, now let's come to the orchestration side, because this is where the repo gets really interesting for bigger work. Unlazy has three modes: solo, which is the single gates file we just covered, orchestrated, and parallel. For big builds, it uses something called the depth tree. You can trigger it with something like {slash} unlazy tree five, refactor the payment module, and verify every migration path. The idea is that layer one is the requested task, and you split it at real domain and component boundaries into leaves, where each leaf is one coherent deliverable with a narrow contract, exact file ownership, and its own gates file. Everything lives under a {dot} unlazy scope folder in your project. There is a plan {dot} md that fixes the interfaces, dependencies, conventions, and file ownership before anything gets dispatched. Then each leaf gets its own ledger, and branches get integration gates on top for interface compatibility, end-to-end behavior, and regressions. And I like that the docs are honest here, too. They explicitly say, "Do not add empty hierarchy just to satisfy a number." If your requested tree depth would create filler leaves, the skill is supposed to state the mismatch and use the closest honest decomposition instead. For parallel work, leaves have to declare OWNS paths, which are repository relative globs of the files they are allowed to write. Two concurrent leaves can never own the same path, and each leaf has to claim its paths through the checker before running. Dispatch is rolling. So, when a verified leaf unblocks another one, the newly ready leaf starts immediately without waiting for unrelated work. And crucially, when a leaf comes back and claims it is done, the parent does not just take its word for it. It reruns the leaf's gates with {dash} {dash} re-verify. Verification flows from the leaves upward, and the final report only happens after the root ledger is satisfied, with every number remeasured right before reporting. Each leaf is also supposed to be worked in four passes. Implement the complete deliverable with no placeholders. Re-rate it as a domain expert, and replace the cheap version of each part. Hunt for correctness, integration, portability, and performance defects, and then apply low-cost polish, and repeat until a full improvement pass finds nothing. There is also one optional extra for Claude code specifically, which is a stop hook. Once installed, whenever the session's ledger still has unmet gates, the hook returns a block decision. So, Claude literally cannot stop and declare victory early. It does not execute any checks itself, and it has a built-in escape valve. After six consecutive blocks with zero ledger progress, it releases, so you cannot get stuck in an infinite loop. And the skill is instructed to never install this hook without your consent, which is the right call. Now, one thing I really respect about this repo is the research section. It cites actual papers on LLM laziness, underthinking and overthinking, and long horizon degradation. Stuff like slob code bench, where the best tested agent passed only about 14.8% of checkpoints on long iterative tasks, and maybe ours time horizon work. But, the readme also plainly says that this research supports the failure modes that motivate the design. It does not prove that unlazy produces some fixed improvement. Earlier versions apparently cited an internal six-run comparison, and the current readme straight-up admits the raw artifacts are not in the repo. So, those numbers should be treated as design history, not a benchmark guarantee. There is even a validation protocol file describing how a defensible rerun would work. In a space full of prompt repos claiming 10x results with zero evidence, that level of honesty is chef's kiss. So, what is my overall take? I think unlazy is genuinely one of the smartest approaches to the half-done work problem right now, because it moves the definition of done out of the model's head and into a file with runnable proof. The approval system shows real security thinking. The whole thing is zero dependency, and the docs are refreshingly honest about what it can and cannot prove. The trade-off is ceremony. For a trivial edit or a quick question, writing a gate ledger is total overkill, and the skill itself says so. This is for substantial work, long refactors, audits, and parallel builds, where the cost of quiet and completeness is way higher than the cost of the ledger. Also, keep in mind that approval is consent, not a sandbox. The checks still run with full access to your machine, so the read before you approve step is is not optional. But for the kind of multi-hour agent runs people are doing these days, this is a really good option for sure. The repo will be linked below and it is free and open source, so definitely give it a try. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you [music] like this video, consider donating through the Super Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this [music] video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye.
